Great question — Medora is a small town with big Badlands scenery and lots of uniquely Western experiences. Below are the best things to do (short description + practical tips and sources).

Top things to do in Medora
1) Drive and explore Theodore Roosevelt National Park (South Unit)
   - What: The 36-mile South Unit scenic loop (starts/ends in Medora) with overlooks, short hikes, prairie dog towns and regular wildlife (bison, wild horses, deer, birds). Plan time for Skyline Vista, Wind Canyon, Painted Canyon overlook and short trail walks. Park open year‑round; some services/visitor centers are seasonal. Practical tip: allow at least a half‑day (more if you plan hikes or lots of photo stops). ([nps.gov](https://www.nps.gov/thingstodo/drive-the-south-unit-scenic-drive.htm?utm_source=openai))

2) See the Medora Musical at the Burning Hills Amphitheatre
   - What: Long‑running outdoor musical revue performed in the historic open‑air Burning Hills Amphitheatre — a summertime highlight and an iconic Medora experience. Book tickets early in summer — evening shows fill up. ([medora.com](https://medora.com/MedoraMusical/?utm_source=openai))

3) Eat the Pitchfork Steak Fondue
   - What: Medora’s famous “pitchfork” steak dinner (served on pitchforks) — a fun, fast dinner option often paired with an evening at the Musical. Reservations / show pairing recommended on busy nights. ([medora.com](https://medora.com/pitchforksteakfondue/?utm_source=openai))

4) Visit the Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library
   - What: Large new Roosevelt library/museum complex just west of Medora (opened in 2026). Good complement to park visits for history, exhibits, and special programming. Check current hours and events before you go. ([trlibrary.com](https://www.trlibrary.com/visit/activities?utm_source=openai))

5) Chateau de Mores State Historic Site & Medora history
   - What: The 1883 chateau and related historic sites interpret Medora’s founding (Marquis de Mores) and local frontier history. There’s also an audio walking tour of town and small museums (Cowboy Hall of Fame, Maltese Cross Cabin, etc.). ([history.nd.gov](https://history.nd.gov/historicsites/chateau/?utm_source=openai))

6) Bully Pulpit Golf Course
   - What: A nationally‑recognized 18‑hole course set through Badlands terrain just south of Medora — spectacular scenery for golfers. Book tee times in advance (seasonal). ([medora.com](https://medora.com/bullypulpit/?utm_source=openai))

7) Outdoor adventures: horseback rides, zipline, Maah Daah Hey access, trails
   - What: Guided trail rides out of Medora, the two‑seat Manitou zipline and access to Maah Daah Hey trailheads and other multi‑hour hikes. Medora is a gateway for Badlands hiking and horseback touring. ([medora.com](https://medora.com/attractions-activities/?utm_source=openai))

8) Point to Point Park / family attractions and small‑town entertainment
   - What: Town activities (mini‑golf, zipline, lazy river in summer at the library complex, Old Town Hall Theater shows, live music in town square, Badlands shooting gallery, shopping and ice cream). Good for families and rainy‑day options. ([medora.com](https://medora.com/attractions-activities/?utm_source=openai))

Suggested sample day / evening
- Morning: South Unit scenic loop with a few short hikes and wildlife viewing (start at the South Unit Visitor Center in Medora). ([nps.gov](https://www.nps.gov/thro/planyourvisit/south-unit.htm?utm_source=openai))
- Late afternoon: Return to town for a walking tour/Chateau visit or a round at Bully Pulpit (golfers).
- Evening: Pitchfork Steak Fondue, then Medora Musical at the Burning Hills Amphitheatre (if in season). ([medora.com](https://medora.com/pitchforksteakfondue/?utm_source=openai))

Practical tips
- Timing: Peak activity and the Medora Musical run in summer (check current season dates/ticket availability). Many in‑town attractions are seasonal; the national park is open year‑round but some visitor services are seasonal — check NPS alerts before you go. ([medora.com](https://medora.com/MedoraMusical/?utm_source=openai))
- Park fees & passes: An entrance fee is required for Theodore Roosevelt NP; accept credit/debit/cards at entrance. Consider an America the Beautiful/pass if visiting multiple federal sites. ([home.nps.gov](https://home.nps.gov/thro/planyourvisit/fees.htm?utm_source=openai))
- Wildlife safety: Watch wildlife from a distance and stay in your vehicle if bison or horses are near the road. Bring water, sunscreen, layered clothing (Badlands weather changes fast) and sturdy shoes for trails. ([nps.gov](https://www.nps.gov/thro/planyourvisit/things2do.htm?utm_source=openai))
- Reservations: Book Musical tickets, Pitchfork dinner and Bully Pulpit tee times in advance during summer, and check hours/closures for the Presidential Library and historic sites. ([medora.com](https://medora.com/MedoraMusical/?utm_source=openai))

- when you plan to go (dates or month) I can check current show schedules, hours, and park alerts and give a more tailored plan (and help with ticket links / where to buy).

Quick logistics
- From Keystone/Mount Rushmore you can build the trip two main ways: 1) through the Black Hills (Custer, Crazy Horse, Deadwood/Spearfish) then north on US‑85 into western North Dakota, or 2) take I‑90 east to Wall/Badlands and then head north. Either way, services and cell coverage thin out once you leave the Black Hills — keep fuel topped up and allow extra time for wildlife pullouts. ([gfp.sd.gov](https://gfp.sd.gov/parks/detail/custer-state-park/?utm_source=openai))

Top picks (short detours / near Mount Rushmore)

Great for wildlife viewing (bison/pronghorn), short hikes and dramatic drives. Plan 1–3 hours to see highlights. ([gfp.sd.gov](https://gfp.sd.gov/parks/detail/custer-state-park/?utm_source=openai))  
- Crazy Horse Memorial — nearby large sculptural memorial with visitor center and museum exhibits; quick stop or 1–2 hour visit if you want the full experience. ([crazyhorsememorial.org](https://crazyhorsememorial.org/visit/plan-your-visit?utm_source=openai))

If you’ve got time for scenic Black Hills detours
- Spearfish Canyon (US‑14A) — a short scenic byway with waterfalls (Roughlock, Bridal Veil, Spearfish Falls) and easy pull‑offs for photos/short walks. Good if you like waterfalls and a cool green canyon contrast to the Badlands. ([blackhillsbadlands.com](https://www.blackhillsbadlands.com/plan/itineraries/summer-scenic-drives-northern-hills/?utm_source=openai))  
- Deadwood — historic Wild West town with Main Street, museums and reenactments if you want history or a break with food/shopping. ([travelsouthdakota.com](https://www.travelsouthdakota.com/iconic-landmarks/deadwood/things-to-do?utm_source=openai))

Expect 1–3+ hours depending on how many overlooks/trails you do. Cell/GPS can be spotty in the park. ([home.nps.gov](https://home.nps.gov/badl/planyourvisit/scenic-driving.htm?utm_source=openai))

- Minuteman Missile National Historic Site — nearby Cold War visitor center and missile-silo exhibits (short, fascinating stop if you’re into history). Tours / mobile tour info at the visitor center. ([nps.gov](https://www.nps.gov/mimi/planyourvisit/directions.htm?utm_source=openai))

Options a little farther / off the direct line (worth it if you like quirky or big‑landscape stops)

([ndtourism.com](https://www.ndtourism.com/regent/attractions-entertainment/family-fun/enchanted-highway?utm_source=openai))

At your destination (quick notes about Theodore Roosevelt NP)
- When you arrive in Medora / Theodore Roosevelt National Park, build time for the South Unit scenic drive (painted canyon overlooks, prairie dog towns, bison along the roads). The park units are spread out — allow several hours to half a day for the South Unit scenic loop. Also note Medora/park is on Mountain Time (you may cross a time zone). ([nps.gov](https://www.nps.gov/npgallery/GetAsset/257b1284-d776-43d5-9a8f-863023a2e520?utm_source=openai))

Sample mini‑itineraries

- Comfortable (1–2 days): Day 1 — Black Hills highlights (Custer State Park, Crazy Horse, Spearfish/Deadwood). Day 2 — drive north via US‑85 into ND with wildlife/grassland stops, arrive Medora in evening and do Park South Unit next morning.

- Medora / Theodore Roosevelt National Park (South Unit) — Painted Canyon Overlook (first Badlands view from the interstate) and the town of Medora (TR National Park visitor center, Medora Musical, cowboy history). Huge scenery; short overlook stops or plan half‑day+ for the scenic drives and wildlife. Exit info: Medora exits ~24–27; Painted Canyon Overlook is at Exit 32. (Good for photography, short walks or a longer Badlands stop.) ([home.nps.gov](https://home.nps.gov/thro/planyourvisit/car.htm?utm_source=openai))

- Enchanted Highway (Gladstone → Regent detour) — a 32‑mile stretch of giant scrap‑metal sculptures (e.g., “Geese in Flight,” “Deer Crossing”) reached from I‑94 near the Gladstone/Regent area; a fun 30–90 minute detour if you like roadside art. ([ndtourism.com](https://www.ndtourism.com/regent/attractions-entertainment/family-fun/enchanted-highway?utm_source=openai))

- Dickinson / Badlands Dinosaur Museum (Dickinson Museum Center) — good family stop, fossils and regional history; convenient services (gas/food) before heading farther west. I‑94 Exit ~61 (Dickinson). Allow 45–90 minutes. ([dickinsongov.com](https://www.dickinsongov.com/museum-center/page/visit-us?utm_source=openai))

- Salem Sue (New Salem) — the “World’s Largest Holstein” sculpture visible from I‑94 (Exit 127); quick photo stop and panoramic prairie views — 10–30 minutes. ([atlasobscura.com](https://www.atlasobscura.com/places/salem-sue/?utm_source=openai))

- Bismarck–Mandan — North Dakota Heritage Center & State Museum (on the State Capitol grounds) for state history and exhibits; Fort Abraham Lincoln State Park (Custer’s home/On‑A‑Slant Mandan village reconstructions) just across the river. Great place for a longer meal + museum stop (1–3 hours). From I‑94 take Exit 159 into Bismarck/Mandan. Top picks (short list)
- Franklin D. Roosevelt Presidential Library & Museum — Hyde Park, NY  
  Why go: First formal presidential library; strong exhibits on the New Deal and WWII; the grounds and FDR’s home nearby add context.

- John F. Kennedy Presidential Library & Museum — Boston, MA  
  Why go: Striking modern architecture and thoughtful exhibits on the 1960s, the Cuban Missile Crisis, civil rights, and JFK’s legacy.

- Abraham Lincoln Presidential Library & Museum — Springfield, IL  
  Why go: One of the nation’s most popular presidential museums — immersive, well-done exhibits about Lincoln, the Civil War, and emancipation.

- Ronald Reagan Presidential Library & Museum — Simi Valley, CA  
  Why go: Large, well-curated museum; standout attractions include a presidential aircraft exhibit and sweeping hilltop views.

- Lyndon B. Johnson Presidential Library — Austin, TX  
  Why go: Excellent civil-rights and Great Society exhibits; close to the Texas State Capitol and LBJ-related sites.

- Richard Nixon Presidential Library & Museum — Yorba Linda, CA  
  Why go: Thorough treatment of Nixon’s career with archival material; well suited to those interested in modern political history.

- Clinton Presidential Center & Library — Little Rock, AR  
  Why go: Attractive riverfront location, engaging exhibits on 1990s policy and life in office, Clinton-era archives.

- George W. Bush Presidential Center — Dallas (SMU), TX  
  Why go: Contemporary exhibitions on policy, 9/11, and leadership; often hosts public programs and lectures.

- Harry S. Truman Library & Museum — Independence, MO  
  Why go: Compact, highly focused look at post–WWII decisions and Truman’s presidency; good for history buffs.

- Dwight D. Eisenhower Presidential Library & Museum — Abilene, KS  
  Why go: Strong WWII and Cold War context, Eisenhower-era artifacts, and the adjacent Eisenhower home and gravesite.

- Herbert Hoover Presidential Library-Museum — West Branch, IA  
  Why go: Good coverage of Hoover’s life and the Great Depression; the site includes his birthplace and memorials.

Museums, archives, and research centers
- Theodore Roosevelt Center at Dickinson State University — a major research center and large digital library of Roosevelt documents and images (free online access to digitized material). Local interpretation and programs

Major accomplishments
- Presidency and political leadership
  - Became president after William McKinley’s assassination (1901) and won election in his own right (1904).  
  - Dramatically expanded the power, visibility, and activism of the executive branch — the “modern presidency.”
- Progressive domestic reforms (the “Square Deal”)

  - Regulation of commerce and public utilities: supported the Hepburn Act (1906) strengthening the Interstate Commerce Commission’s regulatory reach.

  - Panama Canal: engineered U.S. support for Panama’s separation from Colombia (1903) and secured rights to build the Panama Canal — a major strategic and commercial achievement.  
  - Roosevelt Corollary to the Monroe Doctrine (announced 1904): asserted a U.S. policing role in the Western Hemisphere, shaping U.S.–Latin America relations.
- Peace and prestige
  - Won the Nobel Peace Prize (1906) for mediating the end of the Russo–Japanese War — the first U.S. president awarded a Nobel.

Conservation work (one of his signature legacies)
- Philosophy: made conservation a national priority — a pragmatic approach that combined preservation of scenic and scientific sites with wise, managed use of resources. He worked with conservationists such as Gifford Pinchot (scientific forestry) and, sometimes contentiously, preservationists such as John Muir.

Because Theodore Roosevelt National Park is divided into two main sections (the **South Unit** near Medora and the **North Unit** near Watford City), the best nearby attractions depend on where you base your trip. 

Here are the best things to see and do in the surrounding area, grouped by location:

---

### 1. Right at the South Unit (Medora Area)
* **Historic Town of Medora:** The South Unit entrance is located right in Medora, a walkable Old West town with boardwalks, ice cream shops, and western boutiques. 
* **The Medora Musical & Pitchfork Steak Fondue (Summer only):** A legendary North Dakota tradition. Enjoy a ribeye steak cooked on a pitchfork over an open fire, then watch a Broadway-style variety show staged in the open-air Burning Hills Amphitheatre overlooking the Badlands.
* **Château de Mòres State Historic Site:** The 26-room summer home of Antoine de Vallombrosa, the French nobleman (the Marquis de Mòres) who founded Medora in 1883 and named it after his wife. The interpretive center and preserved meatpacking ruins offer fascinating local history.
* **North Dakota Cowboy Hall of Fame:** Located in Medora, this modern museum celebrates Native American culture, ranching, and rodeo history in the Great Plains.

---

### 2. For Outdoor & Trail Enthusiasts
* **Maah Daah Hey Trail:** A world-renowned 144-mile trail connecting the South Unit, Elkhorn Ranch, and North Unit. It is famous among mountain bikers, hikers, and horseback riders for its rugged traverse through the Little Missouri National Grassland.
* **Little Missouri State Park:** Located about an hour northeast of Medora (near Killdeer), this park is often called North Dakota’s hidden gem. It offers some of the most rugged, dramatic badlands terrain in the state, with exceptional hiking and horseback trails.
* **Sullys Creek State Park:** Just south of Medora, this quiet state park is popular for camping, trail riding, and accessing the Little Missouri River for seasonal kayaking or canoeing.

---

### 3. Quirky Sights & Dinosaurs (East along I-94)
* **The Enchanted Highway (Regent to Gladstone):** About 45 minutes east of Medora, this 32-mile stretch of county highway features the world’s largest scrap metal sculptures, including *Geese in Flight* (a Guinness World Record holder), *The Tin Family*, and *Deer Crossing*.
* **Badlands Dinosaur Museum (Dickinson):** Roughly 35 miles east of Medora, Dickinson is the region’s hub. Its museum complex boasts one of the best dinosaur fossil collections on the High Plains, including complete T-rex and Triceratops skeletons found right in the Hell Creek Formation.

---

### 4. Just Across the Montana Border (West along I-94)
* **Makoshika State Park (Glendive, MT):** Just under an hour west of Medora, Makoshika is Montana's largest state park. It showcases towering badland spires, caprocks, and dinosaur fossil quarries, making it a fantastic companion to Theodore Roosevelt National Park.

---

### 5. Historic Sites Near the North Unit (Watford City / Williston)
* **Elkhorn Ranch Unit:** Located halfway between the North and South units along gravel roads. This was Theodore Roosevelt’s "home ranch," chosen for solitude after the tragic deaths of his wife and mother. While only the stone foundation of his cabin remains, the remote, quiet atmosphere is very powerful. *(High-clearance vehicle recommended).*
* **Fort Union Trading Post National Historic Site:** About an hour northwest of Watford City on the Montana border, this reconstructed 1800s fur trading post was the most important trade center on the upper Missouri River, where Assiniboine, Crow, and Blackfeet traded with European merchants.
* **Fort Buford State Historic Site & Missouri-Yellowstone Confluence:** Near Fort Union, this military post was where Chief Sitting Bull surrendered in 1881. Nearby, you can stand at the confluence of the two legendary rivers that shaped the Lewis and Clark expedition.

Medora, North Dakota, is a charming, historic Western town that serves as the gateway to the rugged North Dakota Badlands. Despite its small permanent population, it is packed with outdoor adventure, history, and classic Americana entertainment. 

The top things to do in and around Medora include:

---

### 1. Explore Theodore Roosevelt National Park (South Unit)
The South Unit’s entrance is located right at the edge of town, making Medora the primary base for exploring the park.
* **Scenic Loop Drive:** Take the 36-mile scenic drive (or open sections) to view dramatic Badlands canyons, colorful rock layers, and roaming wildlife.
* **Wildlife Watching:** You are virtually guaranteed to see prairie dog towns, and you have great odds of spotting free-roaming bison herds, wild horses, and pronghorns.
* **Top Hikes:** Don't miss the short **Wind Canyon Trail** (especially at sunset overlooking the Little Missouri River) or the **Ridgeline Nature Trail**. 
* **Maltese Cross Cabin:** Located right behind the South Unit Visitor Center, this is the actual cabin Theodore Roosevelt lived in during his early ranching days in the Dakota Territory.

---

### 2. Attend the *Medora Musical*
Known as the "Greatest Show in the West," this live, outdoor musical variety show is Medora’s centerpiece summer tradition.
* **The Venue:** Performed at the open-air **Burning Hills Amphitheatre**, with the Badlands serving as the natural stage backdrop.
* **The Show:** Runs nightly from early June through early September, celebrating Western heritage, patriotism, and Theodore Roosevelt’s time in North Dakota with song, dance, live horses, and a fireworks finale.

---

### 3. Eat at the Pitchfork Steak Fondue
Held just up the hill from the Burning Hills Amphitheatre before the *Medora Musical*, this is an iconic open-air dining tradition.
* Chefs load 12-ounce ribeyes onto actual pitchforks and submerge them in vats of boiling oil right before your eyes. 
* It's served buffet-style alongside baked potatoes, coleslaw, beans, and cinnamon rolls with panoramic views of the Little Missouri Badlands.

---

### 4. Tour the Chateau de Mores State Historic Site
Learn about Medora’s dramatic founding by the French nobleman Antoine de Vallombrosa, the Marquis de Mores (who named the town after his wife, Medora von Hoffman).
* **The Chateau:** A 26-room, two-story frame building erected in 1883. It is remarkably well-preserved and still contains original furnishings, clothing, and personal belongings.
* **Packing Plant Ruins:** Walk through the nearby site and remaining chimney of the Marquis's ambitious (and ill-fated) refrigerated beef packing enterprise.

---

### 5. Visit the North Dakota Cowboy Hall of Fame
Located downtown, this modern, 15,000-square-foot interpretive center honors North Dakota's Western heritage.
* Exhibits feature Native American history, early homesteaders, ranching life, and a tribute to rodeo champions.
* The outdoor courtyard and patio offer lovely views of the surrounding hills.

---

### 6. Stroll Historic Downtown Medora
Medora’s downtown looks like an authentic Old West movie set with wooden boardwalks and false-front buildings.
* **Rough Riders Hotel:** A historic hotel with modern luxury where Theodore Roosevelt once stayed; check out its massive library featuring over 800 books by and about TR.
* **Shopping & Treats:** Stop into the Medora Fudge & Ice Cream Depot, Western apparel shops, and local gift stores.
* **Theodore’s Dining Room:** Located inside the Rough Riders Hotel, it is one of the premier fine-dining spots in western North Dakota.

---

### 7. Play a Round at Bully Pulpit Golf Course
Ranked among the top public golf courses in the United States, Bully Pulpit winds through meadows, along the Little Missouri River, and dramatically climbs through the Badlands canyons. Holes 14 through 17 take you straight up into the bluffs, offering thrilling tee shots and breathtaking vistas.

---

### 8. Mountain Bike or Hike the Maah Daah Hey Trail
If you want deep wilderness adventure, the world-class **Maah Daah Hey Trail** spans over 140 miles through the Badlands.
* The southernmost trailhead starts near Medora. 
* It is renowned among mountain bikers, endurance runners, and backpackers for its rugged singletrack and pristine prairie scenery.

---

### 9. Family Fun at Point to Point Park
If traveling with children, this park at the base of the amphitheater features:
* The **Little Bully Pulpit Mini Golf Course**
* The **Manitoba Zipline**
* A lazy river, splash pad, jump pillow, and high-ropes course.

---

### Travel Tips
* **Seasonality:** Peak season is **June through Labor Day**, when all shops, tours, and the *Medora Musical* are operating daily. The town becomes much quieter from October through May, though Theodore Roosevelt National Park remains open year-round.
* **Booking:** Book lodging, tickets for the *Medora Musical*, and golf tee times several months in advance if you plan to visit in July or August.

* **Spearfish Canyon Scenic Byway (US-14A):** Instead of staying on the highway between Deadwood and Spearfish, take this 19-mile detour through a towering limestone canyon. It features quick, paved walks to **Bridal Veil Falls** and **Roughlock Falls**, and it barely adds 20–30 minutes of driving.
* **Belle Fourche, SD:** Home to the **Center of the Nation Monument**. While the actual scientific geographic center of the 50 United States is about 20 miles north on private ranch land, Belle Fourche has a large granite compass rose and a visitor center/museum celebrating the landmark right off US-85.

---

### 2. The Big Worthwhile Detour: Devils Tower, WY
* **Extra driving time:** ~1.5 to 2 hours round-trip.
* Just across the Wyoming border, **Devils Tower National Monument** is easily combinable with this route. You can branch west from Spearfish/Belle Fourche on US-14 / WY-24, hike the 1.3-mile paved loop around the base of the massive volcanic monolith, and then head northeast back to US-85. If you haven't seen it, it's well worth the morning detour.

---

### 3. Along US-85 (North Dakota Prairie)

Once you head north of Belle Fourche, the landscape transitions into wide-open, rolling plains and big sky country:

* **Bowman, ND:** The largest town you’ll pass through in southwestern North Dakota. It's a great spot for lunch, coffee, or a fuel stop. The **Pioneer Trails Museum** is surprisingly well-done, featuring regional paleontology (dinosaur fossils), Native American artifacts, and pioneer exhibits.
* **White Butte, ND:** Just east of Amidon, ND, lies the highest natural point in North Dakota (3,506 feet). It requires driving a short stretch of gravel and a 1.4-mile hike across private land (public access is permitted). It's a fun checklist stop for highpointers, but can be skipped if you want to keep moving.

---

### 4. A Quirky Detour: The Enchanted Highway
* **Extra driving time:** ~1 hour each way (east of Belfield / Gladstone).
* If you love American roadside oddities, the **Enchanted Highway** is a 32-mile stretch of two-lane road featuring giant scrap-metal sculptures, including *Geese in Flight* (the world's largest scrap-metal sculpture), *Deer Crossing*, and *Grasshoppers in the Field*. It's located east of Medora, so it works best if you have a leisurely afternoon.

---

### 5. Arriving in Medora (TRNP South Unit Gateway)

Plan to arrive in Medora an hour or two before sunset so you can explore before entering the park:

* **Château de Mores:** A 26-room historic hunting cabin/mansion built in 1883 by the French nobleman Marquis de Mores, who founded the town of Medora and attempted to build a meatpacking empire. 
* **Medora Musical & Pitchfork Fondue (Summer only):** A famous, long-running western musical held in an open-air amphitheater set against the badlands, preceded by steaks fondue-fried on actual pitchforks.

---

### Recommended Route Itineraries

* **Fast & Scenic (Approx. 5.5 hours total):** Mount Rushmore $\rightarrow$ Deadwood $\rightarrow$ Spearfish Canyon $\rightarrow$ Belle Fourche (quick photo) $\rightarrow$ Medora.
* **The "See It All" Route (Approx. 7–8 hours total):** Mount Rushmore $\rightarrow$ Spearfish Canyon $\rightarrow$ Devils Tower $\rightarrow$ Medora.

Interstate 94 spans roughly 350 miles across North Dakota from Fargo in the east to the Montana border in the west. The route transitions from the lush Red River Valley to the rolling prairie, the Missouri River, and finally into the dramatic Badlands. 

Here are the best stops along I-94, organized **east to west**:

* **Fort Abraham Lincoln State Park (Mandan):** Just across the Missouri River, this park features the reconstructed home of General George Custer, military barracks, and the historic **On-A-Slant Indian Village**, with reconstructed Mandan earthlodges.

### 6. New Salem (Mile Marker 127)
* **Salem Sue (The World’s Largest Holstein Cow):** Perched high on School Hill and visible for miles along I-94, this 38-foot-tall fiberglass cow honors the region’s dairy industry. You can drive up the hill to her base for 360-degree views of the surrounding plains.

### 7. Gladstone / The Enchanted Highway (Exit 72)

### 8. Dickinson (Mile Marker 61)

### 9. Painted Canyon Visitor Center (Mile Marker 32)

It offers instant, jaw-dropping panoramic views across the canyon layers, walking paths, and frequent sightings of wild bison grazing along the ridges.

---

### 10. Medora & Theodore Roosevelt National Park (Mile Marker 27)
* **Theodore Roosevelt National Park (South Unit):** The crown jewel of North Dakota. Drive the 36-mile scenic loop to view multi-colored badlands formations, massive prairie dog towns, feral horses, elk, and bison herds. Visit Roosevelt’s original Maltese Cross Cabin at the visitor center.

The North Dakota Badlands—centered around **Theodore Roosevelt National Park** and the historic gateway town of **Medora**—are fantastic for a family trip. The scenery is wild and dramatic, wildlife is everywhere, and Medora offers old-school, kid-focused Western fun. 

Here are the best things to do with kids in the area:

---

### 1. Theodore Roosevelt National Park (South Unit)
*Located right at the edge of Medora.*

* **Watch the Prairie Dog Towns:** This is almost universally a kid favorite. Several prairie dog towns sit right along the 36-mile scenic loop drive. Kids love watching them pop up out of burrows, flick their tails, and "bark" at each other.
* **Spot Wild Horses and Bison:** You won’t have to look hard to spot massive bison herds crossing the road or resting on hillsides. The South Unit is also home to feral wild horses, mule deer, and pronghorns. *(Tip: Remind kids to view them safely from inside the car or at a safe distance!)*
* **Earn a Junior Ranger Badge:** Stop by the South Unit Visitor Center to pick up a free Junior Ranger activity booklet. Kids complete scavenger hunts and educational activities, then get sworn in by a park ranger to earn a wooden badge.
* **Walk through Roosevelt’s Maltese Cross Cabin:** Located right behind the South Unit Visitor Center, this historic cabin gives kids a look at what "roughing it" in the 1880s actually looked like.
* **Easy, Kid-Friendly Hikes:**
  * **Wind Canyon Trail (0.4 miles round-trip):** Short, easy loop with sandstone wind-carved formations and a dramatic view over the Little Missouri River.
  * **Boicourt Overlook Trail (0.2 miles):** A flat, paved trail out to one of the most stunning panoramic views in the park.
  * **Painted Canyon Nature Trail (0.9 miles):** Located at the rest area/overlook off I-94, this takes you right down into the colorful canyon floor.

---

### 2. Family Fun in Medora
*During the summer season (typically Memorial Day through early September), Medora transforms into an energetic Old West family destination.*

* **Point to Point Park:** A family activity park right in Medora featuring:
  * **The Manitou:** An easy-to-ride family roller coaster/zipline.
  * **Little Bully Pulpit Mini Golf:** An 18-hole, themed mini-golf course.
  * **Splash pad & jumping pillow:** Great for younger kids to burn off energy.
* **The Medora Musical:** Held nightly outdoors in the Burning Hills Amphitheatre, this high-energy musical tells the history of the Badlands, Theodore Roosevelt, and the American West. It features live horses on stage, country singing, humor, and fireworks at the finale.
* **Pitchfork Steak Fondue:** Located on the bluff right above the amphitheater, cooks load dozens of 12-oz steaks onto pitchforks and plunge them into giant vats of boiling oil. Kids get a kick out of watching the cooking method (and there are hot dogs/cheeseburgers for pickier eaters).
* **Medora Fudge & Ice Cream Depot:** A must-stop after a day of hiking for homemade fudge, hand-dipped ice cream cones, and old-fashioned sodas.

---

### 3. Hands-On Adventures & Western History
* **Go Horseback Riding:** Take a guided trail ride through the Badlands buttes with **Medora Riding Stables**. They accommodate beginners and older kids for a true cowboy experience.
* **North Dakota Cowboy Hall of Fame:** An interactive, kid-friendly museum in downtown Medora showcasing Native American heritage, rodeo legends, and ranching life.
* **Chateau de Mòres State Historic Site:** Tour the 26-room hunting lodge built in 1883 by the eccentric French nobleman who founded Medora. Kids can see preserved vintage furnishings, old carriages, and period tools.
* **Night Sky Viewing / Stargazing:** The Badlands have minimal light pollution. On a clear night, head to any park pullout to see the Milky Way, meteor showers, and satellites. (The park also hosts ranger-led Astronomy Festivals in late summer).

---

### 4. Exploring the North Unit (Near Watford City)
*If you have time for a day trip about an hour north of Medora:*
* The **North Unit** is much quieter and even more rugged than the South Unit.
* **River Bend Overlook:** One of the most famous views in North Dakota, featuring a stone shelter built by the Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC) that feels like an old castle lookout to kids.
* **Spot Longhorn Cattle:** The North Unit is home to a historical demonstration herd of Texas Longhorn steer, which kids love seeing up close.

---

### Tips for Visiting with Kids
1. **Timing:** Mid-June through August is prime time for Medora’s shows, activities, and dining. If you visit in spring or fall, the park is open, but most town amenities in Medora operate on limited hours or are closed.
2. **Hydration & Sun:** The Badlands get hot and dry quickly in July and August, and shade is rare on trails. Pack twice as much water as you think you need, along with hats and sunscreen.
3. **Wildlife Safety:** Bison look slow, but can sprint up to 35 mph. Bring a pair of binoculars for each kid so they can view wildlife clearly without getting too close.

North Dakota has a rich tapestry of Plains Indian history, pioneer heritage, Badlands culture, and aviation. Here are the best museums to visit across the state:

---

### 1. **North Dakota Heritage Center & State Museum** *(Bismarck)*
* **The Draw:** The state’s flagship museum—often called the “Smithsonian of the Plains.”
* **What to See:** Located on the State Capitol grounds, this massive, modern facility features four distinct galleries spanning billions of years:
  * **Adaptation Gallery:** Impressive dinosaur fossils, including a cast of a *Tyrannosaurus rex* and a 67-million-year-old mummified *Edmontosaurus* named Dakota.
  * **Native Peoples Gallery:** Artifacts and oral histories tracing thousands of years of Indigenous Plains cultures.
  * **Inspiration & Innovation Galleries:** Industrial, agricultural, and space-age history of the state.
* **Bonus:** General admission is free.

---

### 2. **Bonanzaville, USA** *(West Fargo)*
* **The Draw:** One of the premier living-history museums in the Midwest.
* **What to See:** Spanning 12 acres, Bonanzaville features a historic village of more than 40 preserved buildings moved from across the region—including an original 1880s sod house, a 1910 church, a pioneer schoolhouse, and a blacksmith shop. It also houses expansive exhibits showcasing antique tractors, horse-drawn buggies, pioneer medical tools, and vintage airplanes.

---

### 3. **Plains Art Museum** *(Fargo)*
* **The Draw:** The largest art museum in North Dakota.
* **What to See:** Located in a beautifully renovated historic warehouse in downtown Fargo, the museum focuses on contemporary art, regional American art, traditional Native American art, and folk art. It frequently rotates nationally acclaimed exhibitions and offers active community printmaking and ceramics studios.

---

### 4. **Fargo Air Museum** *(Fargo)*
* **The Draw:** An interactive, living aviation museum where many aircraft are kept in operational, flyable condition.
* **What to See:** Two dual hangars house historic warbirds, civilian planes, and modern experimental aircraft ranging from World War II fighters (like the P-51 Mustang) to modern military drones and helicopters. The museum lets visitors get up close to aircraft and features hands-on flight simulators.

---

### 5. **National Buffalo Museum** *(Jamestown)*
* **The Draw:** Dedicated to the cultural, ecological, and economic history of the American Bison.
* **What to See:** The museum overlooks a live herd of bison grazing on the prairie pastures (formerly home to "White Cloud," a legendary albino bison). Inside, you’ll find paleontology exhibits, Native American artifacts, artwork, and historical accounts detailing the near-extinction and recovery of the animal. Just outside stands the famous 26-foot-tall **World's Largest Buffalo** monument.

---

### 6. **Scandinavian Heritage Park** *(Minot)*
* **The Draw:** An outdoor cultural museum celebrating the Nordic heritage of North Dakota’s early immigrants.
* **What to See:** The park honors all five Scandinavian countries (Norway, Sweden, Denmark, Finland, and Iceland). Key highlights include a full-scale replica of the famous **Gol Stave Church** from Norway, an authentic Swedish Dala horse, a 230-year-old timber house (Sigdal House), a Danish windmill, and statues honoring figures like Leif Erikson and Hans Christian Andersen.

---

### 7. **North Dakota Cowboy Hall of Fame & Chateau de Mòres** *(Medora)*
* **The Draw:** Western heritage, Badlands history, and pioneer aristocracy.
* **What to See:**
  * **Cowboy Hall of Fame:** Celebrates the traditions of ranching, rodeo, and the Plains Indians, complete with historical tack, saddles, and cultural artifacts.
  * **Chateau de Mòres State Historic Site:** A 26-room summer home built in 1883 by the eccentric French aristocrat the Marquis de Mòres, who founded the town of Medora. The interpretive center and preserved mansion contain original luxury furnishings of frontier-era nobility.

---

### 8. **Ronald Reagan Minuteman Missile State Historic Site** *(Cooperstown)*
* **The Draw:** Cold War history frozen in time.
* **What to See:** One of the few preserved nuclear missile sites in the United States. You can take an elevator 50 feet underground into the **Oscar-Zero Missile Alert Facility** to view the launch control capsule exactly as it was during the height of the Cold War. Guided tours offer a chilling, fascinating glimpse into the lives of missileers stationed to launch nuclear intercontinental missiles at a moment’s notice.

---

### 9. **Knife River Indian Villages National Historic Site** *(Stanton)*
* **The Draw:** Archaeological preservation of Upper Missouri Native cultures.
* **What to See:** Long before European settlement, the Mandan and Hidatsa peoples lived in thriving, fortified agricultural villages along the Missouri and Knife rivers (where Sakakawea/Sacagawea lived before meeting Lewis and Clark). The museum features an interpretive center with beadwork and trade artifacts, alongside a reconstructed full-scale earthlodge and miles of trails through original village depressions.

While there are 15 official National Archives-administered presidential libraries (along with several state and private ones), a handful consistently stand out to travelers and history buffs for their immersive exhibits, iconic artifacts, architectural beauty, and willingness to tackle complex legacies. 

Here are the presidential libraries most worth visiting, categorized by what makes them special:

---

### 1. The Crowd-Pleaser & Artifact Heavyweight
**Ronald Reagan Presidential Library and Museum** *(Simi Valley, California)*
* **Why it’s worth it:** Perched on a scenic hilltop about an hour northwest of Los Angeles, this is widely considered the most accessible and entertaining library in the system. 
* **Highlights:** 
  * The **Air Force One Pavilion**: You can walk through the actual Boeing 707 (SAM 27000) that carried Reagan, Nixon, and six other presidents, suspended inside a massive glass-walled hangar.
  * A full-scale replica of the Oval Office, an authentic Irish pub dismantled and shipped from Ireland, and an outdoor piece of the Berlin Wall set against sweeping panoramic views.

---

### 2. The Historic Benchmark
**Franklin D. Roosevelt Presidential Library and Museum** *(Hyde Park, New York)*
* **Why it’s worth it:** FDR essentially invented the modern presidential library. Located in the Hudson River Valley, it pairs presidential history with a visit to **Springwood** (FDR’s lifelong estate) and Eleanor Roosevelt’s retreat at **Val-Kill**.
* **Highlights:**
  * Unmatched historical depth covering the Great Depression, the New Deal, and World War II.
  * Personal artifacts like FDR’s specially modified Ford roadster (equipped with hand controls) and original recordings of his "Fireside Chats."

---

### 3. The Modernized Masterpiece
**Harry S. Truman Presidential Library and Museum** *(Independence, Missouri)*
* **Why it’s worth it:** The Truman Library underwent a massive, world-class $30+ million renovation and expansion. It is now one of the most technologically advanced and compelling museums in the country.
* **Highlights:**
  * Powerful, unvarnished interactive exhibits that put you in Truman's shoes as he faced monumental choices: dropping the atomic bomb, launching the Marshall Plan, desegregating the military, and recognizing Israel.
  * Truman and his wife, Bess, are buried in the courtyard, and his simple hometown roots make for an inspiring underdog story.

---

### 4. The Architectural & Visual Standout
**John F. Kennedy Presidential Library and Museum** *(Boston, Massachusetts)*
* **Why it’s worth it:** Designed by legendary architect I.M. Pei, the building itself is a breathtaking modern monument of glass, concrete, and steel perched right on the edge of Boston Harbor.
* **Highlights:**
  * Captures the energy, visual style, and optimism of the early 1960s, covering the Space Race, the Civil Rights Movement, and the Peace Corps.
  * A gripping, tense exhibit dedicated to the 13 days of the **Cuban Missile Crisis**, utilizing original declassified audio tapes from the Oval Office.

---

### 5. The Theatrical & Family-Friendly Pick
**Abraham Lincoln Presidential Library and Museum** *(Springfield, Illinois)*
* **Why it’s worth it:** While operated by the state of Illinois rather than the National Archives, it is often ranked among the best presidential museums in the world. It was designed with the help of former Disney Imagineers, making it exceptionally engaging for adults and children alike.
* **Highlights:**
  * Lifelike silicone figures, holographic theater effects (like the popular *Ghosts of the Library* show), and a full-scale replica of the 1861 White House facade.
  * Springfield is a complete Lincoln pilgrimage: within a short radius, you can visit his home, his law office, his tomb, and the Old State Capitol.

---

### 6. The Deep Dive into Domestic Policy & Upheaval
**Lyndon B. Johnson Presidential Library** *(Austin, Texas)*
* **Why it’s worth it:** Located on the University of Texas at Austin campus, this striking brutalist building houses arguably the most candid look at the friction of the 1960s.
* **Highlights:**
  * The **Great Hall**, with four stories of archive boxes holding 45 million pages of documents framed behind glass.
  * You can listen to LBJ’s infamous secretly recorded phone calls, where he cajoles, flatters, and arm-twists senators into passing the **Civil Rights Act of 1964** and **Voting Rights Act of 1965**.
  * A brutally honest exhibit examining the escalation and cost of the Vietnam War.

---

### Notable Mentions Depending on Your Route:
* **George W. Bush Presidential Center (Dallas, TX):** Features a twisted steel beam from the World Trade Center and the interactive "Decision Points Theater," where visitors vote on real-time crises (like the 2008 financial crash or the invasion of Iraq) before seeing what Bush chose.
* **Dwight D. Eisenhower Presidential Library (Abilene, KS):** Completely overhauled, it is an essential stop for anyone interested in World War II, D-Day logistics, and 1950s Cold War geopolitics.

### Tips for Planning:
* **Time Required:** Most libraries take **2.5 to 4 hours** to visit thoroughly.
* **Compound Visits:** Locations like FDR (Hyde Park) or Lincoln (Springfield) work best as day trips combined with nearby historic homes and estates.

Theodore Roosevelt famously credited the North Dakota Badlands with shaping his character and political identity, saying: *“I never would have been President had it not been for my experience in North Dakota.”* 

Several top places, digital archives, and books detail his time as a rancher, deputy sheriff, and budding conservationist:

---

### 1. In-Person Historic Sites & Museums

* **Theodore Roosevelt National Park (Medora & Watford City, ND)**
  * **Maltese Cross Cabin (South Unit Visitor Center):** Roosevelt’s first residence in Dakota Territory. The original cabin was dismantled, exhibited across the country, and later returned and reconstructed directly behind the South Unit Visitor Center in Medora. You can tour inside to see TR’s desk and period artifacts.
  * **Elkhorn Ranch Unit:** Located about 35 miles north of Medora along the Little Missouri River, this was Roosevelt’s true “home ranch.” While the cabin itself no longer stands, the foundation stones remain in a secluded, quiet river bottom that has been left largely as it was in the 1880s—often called the "Cradle of Conservation."
* **Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library (Medora, ND)**
  * Situated on a scenic butte right outside the national park, this presidential library and museum focuses on Roosevelt’s life, citizenship, and conservation legacy. It features immersive exhibits, personal artifacts (such as his diary marking the deaths of his wife and mother), and interactive programming about his transformation in the Badlands.
* **Chateau de Mores State Historic Site (Medora, ND)**
  * The 26-room summer residence of Antoine de Vallombrosa, the Marquis de Mores—a French nobleman and cattle baron who founded Medora at the same time Roosevelt arrived. Touring the Chateau provides essential context on the Dakota cattle boom of the 1880s and the Marquis’s complicated rivalry and neighborly relations with Roosevelt.

---

### 2. Digital Archives & Research Centers

* **Theodore Roosevelt Center at Dickinson State University (Dickinson, ND & Online)**
  * **Website:** [theodorerooseveltcenter.org](https://www.theodorerooseveltcenter.org/)
  * This is the comprehensive digital archive dedicated to TR. In partnership with the Library of Congress, Harvard, and the National Park Service, the Center has digitized hundreds of thousands of documents, letters, diary entries, and photographs—including Roosevelt's day-to-day ranching correspondence, branding records, and early Dakota writings.
  * The center also maintains a gallery, reading room, and research library on the DSU campus in Dickinson.

---

### 3. Recommended Reading

* **Roosevelt’s Own Memoirs:**
  * ***Hunting Trips of a Ranchman* (1885):** Written while staying in the Badlands, covering his early hunting expeditions and first impressions of the frontier.
  * ***Ranch Life and the Hunting-Trail* (1888):** Featuring classic illustrations by Frederic Remington, this is his love letter to cowboy culture, roundups, and the rugged landscape of western North Dakota.
* **Biographies & Histories:**

### 1. **Early Life & Birthplace**
* **Theodore Roosevelt Birthplace National Historic Site (New York, NY)**  
  Located at 28 East 20th Street in Manhattan, this is a reconstructed four-story brownstone on the site where Roosevelt was born in 1858 and lived until he was 14. It features period-furnished rooms and exhibits detailing his childhood and struggle with asthma.

---

### 2. **Ranching & Conservation in the West**
* **Theodore Roosevelt National Park (Medora, ND)**  
  Roosevelt arrived in the Dakota Territory in 1883 to hunt bison, and he soon invested in cattle ranching. The park preserves the Badlands landscape that deeply influenced his philosophy on conservation:
  * **Maltese Cross Cabin:** Roosevelt’s first ranch cabin, now preserved near the park’s South Unit Visitor Center.
  * **Elkhorn Ranch Unit:** The remote site along the Little Missouri River where Roosevelt built his primary ranch house after the tragic deaths of his wife and mother on the same day in 1884.

---

### 3. **The Rough Riders & Military Career**
* **The Menger Hotel (San Antonio, TX)**  
  During the Spanish-American War in 1898, Roosevelt stayed at this historic hotel and used its bar to recruit cowboys, frontiersmen, and polo players for the 1st U.S. Volunteer Cavalry, famously known as the "Rough Riders."

---

### 4. **Ascension to the Presidency**
* **Theodore Roosevelt Inaugural National Historic Site (Buffalo, NY)**  
  Also known as the **Ansley Wilcox House**, this is where Roosevelt took the oath of office as the 26th President on September 14, 1901, following the assassination of President William McKinley at the Pan-American Exposition.

---

### 5. **Home, "Summer White House," and Burial Site**
* **Sagamore Hill National Historic Site (Oyster Bay, Long Island, NY)**  
  Roosevelt’s beloved 23-room Queen Anne-style home served as his family residence and as the "Summer White House" from 1902 to 1908. It remains filled with his original furniture, hunting trophies, and personal library. Roosevelt died here in 1919.
* **Youngs Memorial Cemetery (Oyster Bay, NY)**  
  Located less than two miles from Sagamore Hill, this cemetery is the final resting place of Theodore and his second wife, Edith Roosevelt.

---

### 6. **Presidential Retreat**
* **Pine Knot (Albemarle County, VA)**  
  A simple, rustic two-story wooden cabin purchased by the Roosevelts in 1905 to escape Washington, D.C. TR used it as a secluded retreat for birdwatching, hunting, and relaxation during his presidency.

---

### 7. **Major Memorials & Monuments**
* **Theodore Roosevelt Island (Washington, D.C.)**  
  An 88-acre wooded island in the Potomac River, managed as a living memorial to Roosevelt's conservation legacy. It features miles of trails and a central plaza with a 17-foot bronze statue of Roosevelt.
* **Mount Rushmore National Memorial (Keystone, SD)**  
  Sculptor Gutzon Borglum selected Roosevelt to be carved into the Black Hills alongside George Washington, Thomas Jefferson, and Abraham Lincoln to represent the development and growth of the United States and the Panama Canal.

Whether the **Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library** is worth visiting depends largely on your travel style and interests, but for most travelers—especially history enthusiasts, architecture fans, and national park visitors—**it is well worth the trip.** 

Located in **Medora, North Dakota**, the library offers a very different experience from traditional presidential libraries.

---

### Why It’s Worth Visiting

* **The Unique Setting:** Roosevelt famously said, *"I never would have been President if it had not been for my experiences in North Dakota."* Unlike urban or suburban presidential libraries, this one is situated directly in the rugged Badlands landscape where a young TR rebuilt his health, spirit, and grit after personal tragedy. 
* **Striking, Sustainable Architecture:** Designed by the renowned architectural firm Snøhetta, the building is integrated seamlessly into a Badlands butte. Featuring green rooftops you can walk across, rammed-earth styling reflecting the local geology, and zero-net-energy sustainability goals under the Living Building Challenge, the facility itself is an architectural attraction.
* **Modern, Immersive Exhibits:** Far from static glass cases, the library features interactive Narrative and Adventure Galleries, personalized digital "Trailblazer" elements, and multi-sensory storytelling exploring Roosevelt's legacy as a reformer, conservationist, and complex historical figure. 
* **Built-in National Park Trip:** The library sits just minutes from the South Unit entrance of **Theodore Roosevelt National Park**. Visiting allows you to easily combine the museum with wildlife viewing (bison herds, wild horses, prairie dogs) and scenic Badlands hikes.
* **Historic Medora:** Medora itself is a charming western town featuring historic sites, local dining, outdoor trails (like the Maah Daah Hey Trail), and the famous outdoor *Medora Musical* during summer months.

---

### Drawbacks & Considerations

* **Remote Location:** Medora is fairly isolated—roughly a 2-hour drive west of Bismarck and about 4.5 hours from Fargo or Rapid City, South Dakota. It is rarely a standalone day-trip and is best experienced as part of a dedicated road trip.
* **Timed-Entry Reservations:** Because of daily capacity limits, you will generally need to plan ahead and reserve timed-entry tickets online rather than just dropping in.
* **Seasonality:** Summer and early autumn are the optimal times to visit. Medora is fully operational during those months, whereas western North Dakota winters can be harsh, and local town amenities run on reduced schedules.

---

### The Verdict

* **Go if:** You are road-tripping through the northern Great Plains, visiting Theodore Roosevelt National Park, or have an interest in TR’s life, conservation history, and innovative modern architecture. 
* **Skip (or postpone) if:** You are pressed for time, cannot easily reach western North Dakota, or prefer traditional archive-heavy historical museums over immersive, technology-driven exhibits.

The institution recommends allowing around 3.5 hours to experience the core galleries, with additional time depending on your pace:

* **Main Exhibition Galleries (2 to 2.5 hours):** The museum features extensive, immersive exhibits covering Theodore Roosevelt’s life, conservation legacy, presidency, and his transformative time in the North Dakota Badlands. 
* **Interactive Displays & Media (30 to 45 minutes):** Time for hands-on stations, films, and multimedia installations.
* **Outdoor Boardwalks & Architecture (30 to 60 minutes):** The library was designed by Snøhetta to blend directly into the rugged Badlands landscape. Walking the elevated pathways, viewing platforms, and surrounding native prairie is a significant part of the experience.
* **Café & Gift Shop (20 to 30 minutes):** Time to grab a drink, light bite, or browse books and merchandise.

---

### Key Tips for Planning Your Visit
* **Timed-Entry Tickets:** Entry is managed via timed tickets to prevent crowding; booking online in advance is strongly recommended, particularly during the peak summer and fall seasons.
* **Minimum Time:** The final timed entry of the day is 90 minutes before closing, but visiting with that little time will feel very rushed.
* **Combine with Medora & the National Park:** If you are planning a full-day itinerary, you can easily pair a 3- to 4-hour visit at the library with a scenic drive or hike through the South Unit of Theodore Roosevelt National Park right next door.

Theodore Roosevelt, the 26th President of the United States (serving from 1901 to 1909), was a transformative leader whose dynamic personality and expansive view of executive power ushered in the modern American presidency. 

Below is an overview of his major accomplishments, his groundbreaking conservation work, and his enduring legacy.

---

### 1. Major Accomplishments

Roosevelt believed the president should act as a "steward of the people." His domestic platform, known as the **Square Deal**, aimed to balance the competing interests of labor, capital, and the public under three core pillars: consumer protection, corporate regulation, and conservation.

#### Domestic Policy & Trust-Busting
* **Regulating Monopolies ("Trust-Busting"):** Roosevelt directed the Department of Justice to bring dozens of antitrust suits under the Sherman Antitrust Act. His administration famously broke up the **Northern Securities Company** (a railroad monopoly) and pursued trusts in oil, beef, and tobacco, earning him the nickname "The Trust Buster" (though he distinguished between "good trusts" that served the public interest and "bad trusts" that abused monopoly power).
* **Consumer Protection:** Spurred by public outcry after Upton Sinclair published *The Jungle*, Roosevelt pushed Congress to pass two landmark laws in 1906:
  * **The Meat Inspection Act:** Required federal inspection of meat products and established strict sanitation standards.
  * **The Pure Food and Drug Act:** Banned misbranded or adulterated food and medicine, laying the foundation for what became the Food and Drug Administration (FDA).
* **Fair Labor Mediation:** During the **1902 Anthracite Coal Strike**, Roosevelt broke precedent by refusing to automatically use federal troops to break the strike. Instead, he forced both mine owners and the union to submit to federal arbitration, securing wage increases and shorter workdays for the miners.
* **Railroad Regulation:** He signed the **Elkins Act (1903)** and the **Hepburn Act (1906)**, which empowered the Interstate Commerce Commission (ICC) to set maximum railroad shipping rates and outlawed preferential rebate practices.

#### Foreign Policy & Diplomacy
Roosevelt advocated for a muscular foreign policy summarized by his famous proverb: *"Speak softly and carry a big stick."*
* **The Panama Canal:** Roosevelt facilitated Panamanian independence from Colombia in 1903 to secure the rights to build the Panama Canal, vastly reducing maritime transit times between the Atlantic and Pacific oceans.
* **Roosevelt Corollary to the Monroe Doctrine (1904):** He declared that the U.S. had the right to intervene as an "international police power" in Latin American nations to prevent European intervention, cementing American dominance in the Western Hemisphere.
* **Nobel Peace Prize (1906):** Roosevelt mediated the end of the Russo-Japanese War, negotiating the **Treaty of Portsmouth**. He became the first American to win a Nobel Peace Prize.
* **The Great White Fleet:** Between 1907 and 1909, he sent an armada of 16 modern U.S. Navy battleships on a world tour to demonstrate American naval prowess and global reach.

---

### 2. Conservation Work

Roosevelt considered conservation his greatest and most lasting domestic achievement. Influenced by figures like naturalist John Muir and U.S. Chief Forester Gifford Pinchot, he shifted national policy from exploiting natural resources to conserving and managing them for future generations.

During his presidency, Roosevelt placed roughly **230 million acres of land under federal protection**:

* **The Antiquities Act of 1906:** Roosevelt signed this law giving the president unilateral power to designate historic landmarks, historic and prehistoric structures, and other objects of historic or scientific interest as National Monuments. He immediately used it to protect sites like **Devils Tower**, the **Grand Canyon**, and **Muir Woods**.
* **Creation of the U.S. Forest Service (USFS):** Established in 1905, the USFS professionalized public land management. Roosevelt expanded federal forest reserves from roughly 43 million acres to nearly 150 million acres.
* **National Parks and Wildlife Sanctuaries:**
  * Created **5 National Parks** (Crater Lake, Wind Cave, Sullys Hill, Mesa Verde, and Platt).
  * Established **18 National Monuments**.
  * Created the first federal bird reserve (**Pelican Island**, Florida, in 1903), eventually establishing **51 Federal Bird Reserves**.
  * Established **4 National Game Preserves**.
* **Newlands Reclamation Act (1902):** Funded irrigation and water-management projects in 20 arid western states, paving the way for sustainable settlement and agriculture.

---

### 3. Legacy and Impact

Theodore Roosevelt left an indelible mark on the nature of American governance, environmentalism, and foreign affairs:

* **Creation of the Modern Presidency:** Before Roosevelt, Congress dominated national politics, and presidents largely adhered to narrow constitutional interpretations. Roosevelt popularized the concept of the **"bully pulpit,"** using the presidency as a platform to rally public opinion and steer the national legislative agenda.
* **Father of American Conservation:** His public land policies established the framework for the modern National Park Service, U.S. Forest Service, and Fish and Wildlife Service, preserving many of America's most iconic landscapes.
* **Foundation for Progressive Reform:** His trust-busting, labor arbitration, and regulatory reforms demonstrated that the federal government could serve as an arbiter between corporate power and working citizens. His ideas later directly influenced both Woodrow Wilson’s "New Freedom" and his fifth cousin Franklin D. Roosevelt's "New Deal."
* **Global Power Status:** By strengthening the navy and expanding overseas diplomatic engagements, Roosevelt solidified the transition of the United States from an isolated regional actor to an influential world superpower.
*

President Theodore Roosevelt’s **“Square Deal”** was his signature domestic policy during his presidency (1901–1909). Rooted in the Progressive Era, the Square Deal was based on the idea that the federal government should act as an impartial referee to ensure fairness for all Americans—preventing wealthy corporations from abusing their power while also discouraging violent, radical labor strikes. 

Roosevelt summed up the philosophy by stating that he did not favor any particular group, but aimed to guarantee that every citizen received a **“square deal”**—an honest and fair shake under the law.

The policy’s main goals and actions are traditionally organized around the **“Three Cs”**:

---

### 1. Control of Corporations (Trust-Busting and Regulation)
During the Gilded Age, monopolistic trusts dominated major industries and stifled competition. Roosevelt did not believe all big businesses were inherently bad—he recognized that scale could bring efficiency. However, he drew a firm distinction between **“good trusts”** (which provided fair prices and public service) and **“bad trusts”** (which abused market power, price-gouged, and crushed competition).

* **Enforcing the Sherman Antitrust Act:** Roosevelt revitalized the mostly dormant 1890 Sherman Act. His administration filed over 40 antitrust suits, most famously breaking up J.P. Morgan’s railroad monopoly, the **Northern Securities Company**, in 1904.
* **Railroad Regulation:** Roosevelt pushed Congress to pass the **Elkins Act of 1903** (banning discriminatory railroad rebates favored by big shippers) and the **Hepburn Act of 1906** (empowering the Interstate Commerce Commission to set maximum railroad freight rates).
* **Intervention in the 1902 Anthracite Coal Strike:** When coal miners struck for better wages and hours, threatening winter fuel supplies, Roosevelt intervened directly. Instead of using troops to break the strike (as previous presidents had done), he brought mine owners and union leaders to arbitration, securing a wage increase and a shorter workday—the first time a president acted as an even-handed mediator between capital and labor.

---

### 2. Consumer Protection
Before Roosevelt, the principle of *caveat emptor* ("buyer beware") largely governed American commerce. Spurred by investigative journalists known as "muckrakers"—most notably Upton Sinclair, whose 1906 novel *The Jungle* exposed nauseating sanitary conditions in the meatpacking industry—Roosevelt pressured Congress to hold manufacturers accountable.

* **Meat Inspection Act (1906):** Mandated strict federal sanitary standards for meat processing and instituted federal inspections of livestock before and after slaughter.
* **Pure Food and Drug Act (1906):** Prohibited the manufacture and sale of adulterated or mislabeled food and drugs, and required truth-in-labeling for active ingredients, laying the groundwork for the modern Food and Drug Administration (FDA).

---

### 3. Conservation of Natural Resources
Roosevelt considered conservation to be his most enduring and vital domestic legacy. A passionate outdoorsman, he believed America’s natural resources were finite and had to be managed scientifically for future generations rather than pillaged by unregulated commercial exploitation (such as clear-cut logging and unchecked mining).

* **Public Lands & Forest Reserves:** Working closely with Gifford Pinchot (the first head of the newly created U.S. Forest Service), Roosevelt placed roughly **230 million acres** of land under federal protection.
* **National Parks and Monuments:** Roosevelt created 5 new national parks, 18 national monuments, 51 federal bird sanctuaries, and 150 national forests.
* **Antiquities Act of 1906:** Roosevelt signed this law enabling presidents to quickly designate public lands as national monuments to preserve historic and natural landmarks (such as the Grand Canyon and Devils Tower).
* **Newlands Reclamation Act (1902):** Funded irrigation and water-management projects to develop agricultural lands across the arid American West.

---

### Legacy of the Square Deal
The Square Deal fundamentally transformed the American presidency and the role of the federal government. It marked the end of the strict *laissez-faire* (hands-off) era and established the precedent that the president and federal agencies could actively intervene in the economy to protect public health, check corporate monopolies, and safeguard the environment. It also paved the rhetorical and ideological way for later reform movements, including his fifth cousin Franklin D. Roosevelt's **New Deal** in the 1930s.

**Theodore Roosevelt** served as the 26th president of the United States from **September 14, 1901, to March 4, 1909**. 

He first assumed the presidency following the assassination of President William McKinley in September 1901 (becoming the youngest person to hold the office at age 42) and was subsequently elected to a full term in his own right in 1904.

During his two terms, Roosevelt championed progressive domestic policies under his slogan, the **"Square Deal"** (promising fairness for workers, consumers, and business), and pursued an assertive foreign policy best captured by his motto, *"Speak softly and carry a big stick."*

---

### Major Milestones of His Administration

#### 1. Domestic Milestones & Progressive Reforms ("The Square Deal")

* **Trust-Busting and Corporate Regulation:**
  * **Northern Securities Co. v. United States (1904):** Roosevelt directed his Justice Department to invoke the Sherman Antitrust Act to break up J.P. Morgan’s railroad monopoly, establishing his reputation as a "trust-buster." His administration went on to initiate dozens of suits against monopolies, distinguishing between "good trusts" and "bad trusts."
  * **Elkins Act (1903) & Hepburn Act (1906):** Strengthened the Interstate Commerce Commission (ICC), outlawing railroad rebates to favored shippers and granting the federal government the power to set maximum railroad shipping rates.

* **Consumer Health and Safety:**
  * **Meat Inspection Act (1906) & Pure Food and Drug Act (1906):** In response to public outrage fueled by Upton Sinclair’s muckraking novel *The Jungle*, Roosevelt pushed through landmark legislation mandating sanitary standards in slaughterhouses and requiring accurate labeling on foods and medicines. This laid the foundation for what became the modern Food and Drug Administration (FDA).

* **Federal Labor Mediation:**
  * **Anthracite Coal Strike of 1902:** When coal miners went on strike ahead of the winter of 1902, Roosevelt intervened—not by siding with mine owners (as past presidents had done), but by threatening to take over the mines with federal troops if owners did not negotiate. This established a precedent of the federal government acting as an impartial mediator in labor disputes.

* **Environmental Conservation:**
  * Widely regarded as Roosevelt’s most enduring legacy, he drastically expanded the federal role in conserving America's natural resources alongside U.S. Forest Service chief Gifford Pinchot.
  * **Antiquities Act of 1906:** Allowed presidents to designate landmarks and prehistoric structures as national monuments by proclamation (e.g., Devils Tower, the Grand Canyon, and Muir Woods).
  * Roosevelt placed approximately **230 million acres** of land under public protection, establishing 5 national parks, 18 national monuments, 150 national forests, and 51 federal bird reserves.

---

#### 2. Foreign Policy Milestones ("Big Stick" Diplomacy)

* **The Panama Canal (1903–1904):**
  * After Colombia rejected a treaty allowing the U.S. to build a trans-isthmian canal in its province of Panama, Roosevelt backed Panamanian separatists with U.S. naval support. Panama achieved independence in 1903 and quickly signed the **Hay-Bunau-Varilla Treaty**, granting the U.S. construction rights to the Panama Canal Zone. Construction began in 1904.

* **The Roosevelt Corollary to the Monroe Doctrine (1904):**
  * Roosevelt asserted that the United States had the right to act as an "international police power" in the Western Hemisphere to prevent European intervention in debt-ridden or unstable Latin American nations.

* **Mediation of the Russo-Japanese War (1905):**
  * Roosevelt hosted peace talks in Portsmouth, New Hampshire, to broker an end to the Russo-Japanese War. His negotiation of the **Treaty of Portsmouth** earned him the **Nobel Peace Prize in 1906**, making him the first American to win the award.

* **Voyage of the "Great White Fleet" (1907–1909):**
  * Roosevelt ordered 16 U.S. Navy battleships on a 14-month circumnavigation of the globe to showcase America’s growing status as a blue-water naval superpower.

* **Gentlemen’s Agreement of 1907:**
  * Roosevelt negotiated an informal agreement with Japan where the U.S. agreed not to impose formal restrictions on Japanese immigration or segregate Japanese schoolchildren in California, in exchange for Japan restricting the emigration of laborers to the United States.

The four U.S. presidents carved into Mount Rushmore in South Dakota are:

1. **George Washington** (1st President)
2. **Thomas Jefferson** (3rd President)
3. **Theodore Roosevelt** (26th President)
4. **Abraham Lincoln** (16th President)

---

### Why Theodore Roosevelt Was Included

The sculptor of Mount Rushmore, **Gutzon Borglum**, chose the four presidents to represent key stages of American history:

* **Washington** represented the **birth** of the nation.
* **Jefferson** represented the **growth** and expansion of the nation (through the Louisiana Purchase).
* **Lincoln** represented the **preservation** of the nation (through the Civil War).
* **Roosevelt** was selected to represent the **development** of the United States.

Specifically, Borglum included Roosevelt for several key reasons:

1. **Rise as a Global Power:** Roosevelt led the country at the turn of the 20th century as it transitioned into a major modern world power. His leadership in the construction of the Panama Canal—which linked the Atlantic and Pacific oceans—symbolized America’s technological prowess and global influence.
2. **Conservation Legacy:** Roosevelt placed roughly 230 million acres of land under federal protection, creating national forests, parks, bird reserves, and game preserves. As Mount Rushmore is located in the rugged Black Hills of South Dakota, honoring the "Conservation President" resonated deeply with the spirit of the American West.
3. **Economic and Social Reform:** Known as a "trust-buster," Roosevelt championed his "Square Deal," regulating large monopolies, protecting workers, and ensuring economic fairness for everyday citizens during a period of rapid industrial growth.
4. **Personal Connection with Borglum:** Borglum had a personal admiration for Roosevelt, having met and campaigned for him. Borglum viewed Roosevelt as the embodiment of the energetic, rugged, and forward-looking 20th-century American spirit.

Theodore Roosevelt was president from **1901 to 1909**. 

The exact dates of his administration were:
* **Start date:** September 14, 1901 (assuming office following the death of President William McKinley)
* **End date:** March 4, 1909 (concluding with the inauguration of William Howard Taft)

The four U.S. presidents depicted on Mount Rushmore are:

1. **George Washington**
2. **Thomas Jefferson**
3. **Theodore Roosevelt**
4. **Abraham Lincoln**

---

### Why Theodore Roosevelt Was Included

Sculptor Gutzon Borglum conceived Mount Rushmore as a monument representing the first 150 years of American history, choosing each president to symbolize a foundational theme:

* **George Washington** represented the **birth** of the nation.
* **Thomas Jefferson** represented the **growth** and expansion of the nation (notably through the Louisiana Purchase).
* **Abraham Lincoln** represented the **preservation** of the nation through the Civil War.
* **Theodore Roosevelt** was chosen to represent the **development** and emergence of the United States as a 20th-century world power.

Specific reasons for Roosevelt's inclusion include:

* **Rise as a Global Economic and Naval Power:** Under Roosevelt's leadership, the United States asserted itself on the world stage. Most notably, he spearheaded the construction of the **Panama Canal**, which linked the Atlantic and Pacific oceans, fundamentally transforming global trade and national defense.
* **Economic Reform and the "Square Deal":** Roosevelt took on monopolies and corporate trusts, championing consumer protections and labor rights to ensure fairness for everyday American workers.
* **Leadership in Conservation:** Roosevelt set aside hundreds of millions of acres of public land, establishing national forests, wildlife refuges, and monuments, leaving a profound natural legacy that resonated strongly with the monument's rugged outdoor setting.
* **Borglum’s Personal Connection:** Borglum was a strong personal admirer and acquaintance of Roosevelt. He had actively supported Roosevelt’s 1912 presidential campaign under the Progressive ("Bull Moose") Party, which cemented his belief that Roosevelt was the defining president of early 20th-century America.
